title: Unit 3 Quiz · Predictive Modeling Techniques
instructions: 30 questions, 31 marks. You have 30 minutes; the quiz submits itself when time runs out.
Questions and options are shuffled, so your neighbour's screen will not match yours.
Multi-select questions need ALL correct options for the marks. Ordering questions give part marks for each item in the right place.
After submitting you will see your score and an explanation for every question.

questions.q: Which task is a CLASSIFICATION problem?
options: Predicting whether a loan applicant will default (yes/no)
Predicting next month’s electricity bill in rupees
Predicting the selling price of a used car
questions.explain: A yes/no target is a category, so it is classification. The others predict numbers (regression).

questions.q: Logistic regression is used for:
options: Classification: it predicts the probability of a category
questions.explain: Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier: it outputs a probability between 0 and 1.

questions.q: For five cars, Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = −7.90 and Σ(x − x̄)² = 10. What is the least-squares slope b?
With slope b = −0.79, x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 6.38, the intercept a is:
SSE = 0.067 and SST = 6.308. What is R²?
Least squares chooses the line that minimises:
options: The sum of squared residuals Σ(y − ŷ)²
The number of points above the line
questions.explain: That is the definition of ordinary least squares.

questions.q: In the car model, tier_Premium = +11.43 with Budget as the baseline. This means:
options: A Premium car is predicted ₹11.43 lakh more than an otherwise identical Budget car
Premium cars lose ₹11.43 lakh per year
There are 11.43 times more Premium cars
questions.explain: A dummy coefficient compares that category with the baseline, holding all other features fixed.

questions.q: Price = 5.993 − 0.462×age − 0.0074×km_thousand − 0.310×owners + 3.125×tier_Mid. A 5-year-old Mid petrol manual with 60,000 km and 1 owner is predicted at about:
Why use adjusted R² rather than R² to compare models with different numbers of features?
options: R² never decreases when a feature is added, even a useless one; adjusted R² penalises extra features
R² cannot be computed for multiple regression
questions.explain: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k − 1) only rises if a new feature improves the fit enough.

questions.q: Test RMSE = 0.885 and MAE = 0.697 (₹ lakh). Which statement is true?
options: RMSE is larger because squaring gives big errors extra weight
MAE is always larger than RMSE
RMSE is the percentage of variation explained
questions.explain: RMSE ≥ MAE always; a big gap means some large individual errors.

questions.q: A residual plot shows a clear funnel shape (spread grows with the prediction). Which assumption is violated?
questions.explain: A funnel means non-constant variance (heteroscedasticity). A log of the target often helps.

questions.q: The logistic coefficient for support_calls is b = 0.3986. Its odds ratio e^b ≈ 1.49 means:
options: Each extra support call multiplies the odds of churning by about 1.49
Each call increases the churn probability by 49 percentage points
questions.explain: e^b is an odds ratio. The change in probability depends on where you start on the S-curve.

questions.q: Autopay has b = −0.584 (odds ratio 0.558). Interpretation:
options: Autopay customers have about 44% lower odds of churning, other things equal
Autopay customers are 55.8% of the data
questions.explain: 1 − 0.558 ≈ 0.44, so the odds are 44% lower.

questions.q: If the linear part of a logistic model is z = 0, the predicted probability is:
Why not fit an ordinary straight line to a 0/1 churn target?
options: A straight line can predict values below 0 or above 1, which are impossible probabilities
questions.explain: Logistic regression models the log-odds as linear and maps it into (0, 1) with the sigmoid.

questions.q: A node has 238 churners out of 1,050 customers (p = 0.227). Its Gini impurity is about:
A pure node (all customers in one class) has Gini impurity:
Children: 907 customers with Gini 0.313 and 143 with Gini 0.491. The weighted Gini after the split is about:
Which setting helps stop a decision tree from overfitting?
options: Limiting max_depth or requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf
questions.explain: Shallower trees and larger leaves cannot memorise individual customers.

questions.q: Which tree algorithm uses the chi-square test to choose splits and is SPSS’s default?
questions.explain: CHAID = Chi-squared Automatic Interaction Detection. CART uses Gini; ID3 uses entropy.

questions.q: What is the Euclidean distance between (6, 3) and (8, 2)?
KNN with k = 1 scored 98.4% on training data but 69.8% on test data. This is:
options: Overfitting: the model memorised individual training points
questions.explain: A huge train–test gap is the signature of overfitting.

questions.q: Why must features be scaled before KNN?
options: Distances are dominated by features with large numeric ranges, such as monthly charge in rupees
KNN only accepts values between 0 and 1
questions.explain: Without scaling, a ₹100 difference outweighs a 10-month or 5-call difference. Unscaled KNN recall fell to 4.9%.

questions.q: What does the ‘naïve’ in Naïve Bayes refer to?
options: It assumes features are independent of each other given the class
It can only use two features
questions.explain: That assumption lets the per-feature probabilities be multiplied.

questions.q: Naïve Bayes scores: churn = 0.01514, stay = 0.00922. What is P(churn | evidence)?
Gaussian Naïve Bayes gave a new customer P(churn) = 0.936, while the other models gave 0.60–0.73. A likely reason:
options: Correlated features are treated as independent, so evidence is counted twice and probabilities become over-confident
The customer was in the training set
questions.explain: Support calls and satisfaction are correlated (r = −0.31); NB multiplies both as if independent.

questions.q: Arrange the model-building steps in order.
options: Split into train and test sets
Fit preprocessing on the training data
Evaluate once on the test set
questions.explain: Split before learning anything from the data; evaluate on the test set only at the end.

questions.q: Why use stratify=y when splitting the churn data?
options: To keep the same churn rate (22.7%) in both the training and test sets
To sort the data by churn
To remove churners from the test set
To make the split random every time
questions.explain: With an imbalanced target, a plain random split could leave very different churn rates in each part.

questions.q: Which of these is DATA LEAKAGE?
options: Scaling features with the mean and sd of the whole dataset before splitting
Training a decision tree with max_depth = 3
questions.explain: Statistics from the test rows have shaped the training data, so test scores look better than reality.

questions.q: At a 0.5 cut-off, all four churn models had about 76–78% accuracy but caught only 9–28% of churners. Why?
options: Only 22.7% of customers churn, so few reach a 50% predicted probability; accuracy is dominated by the many stayers
The models were trained on the test set
Recall and accuracy are the same thing
questions.explain: Imbalanced targets make accuracy misleading; Unit 4 adjusts the threshold and uses precision, recall and ROC.
